title: YOUR PASTOR IS NOT YOUR MEDIATOR—JESUS IS
paragraphs: YOUR PASTOR IS NOT YOUR MEDIATOR—JESUS IS

The person behind the pulpit may shepherd you, teach you, correct you, pray with you, and point you toward God—but there is only One who can stand between a guilty sinner and a holy God. And His name is Jesus.
There is a dangerous moment that can happen inside a church without anyone noticing.
The music is beautiful.
The sermon is powerful.
The pastor is gifted.

You trust him. You respect him. Maybe his preaching helped pull you out of one of the darkest seasons of your life. Maybe he prayed for your marriage when it was collapsing. Maybe his words confronted an addiction nobody else knew about. Maybe God used his ministry to bring you back after years of wandering.
And slowly—almost invisibly—something shifts.
You stop merely appreciating the shepherd.
You begin depending on him for what only the Savior can give.
You feel close to God when your pastor notices you.
You feel forgotten by God when your pastor does not.
You need his approval before you feel spiritually secure.
You assume his prayers somehow reach heaven more effectively than yours.
When your conscience is crushed, your first instinct is not always to run to Christ but to find a spiritual person who can somehow make things right between you and God.
And perhaps the most revealing question is this:
If your pastor disappeared tomorrow, would your relationship with Jesus collapse with him?
That question may sting.
But sometimes the questions that hurt are the ones that expose where our trust has quietly moved.
Scripture gives us a sentence so simple that it destroys every attempt to place another human being in the position belonging exclusively to Christ:
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 2:5, KJV
The Greek is even more striking:
εἷς γὰρ Θεός, εἷς καὶ μεσίτης Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἄνθρωπος Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς
heis gar Theos, heis kai mesitēs Theou kai anthrōpōn, anthrōpos Christos Iēsous.
One God.
One Mediator.
The Greek word μεσίτης — mesitēs refers to a mediator, an intermediary, one who stands between parties in order to bring about reconciliation or establish a covenant relationship.
And Paul does not leave the identity of that Mediator open for speculation.
Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς.
Christ Jesus.
Not your pastor.
Not your favorite preacher.
Not the Christian influencer whose videos you watch every morning.
Not the evangelist whose sermons make you cry.
Not the theologian whose books transformed your thinking.
Not the person who baptized you.
Not the person who discipled you.
Not even the most faithful spiritual leader you have ever known.
Jesus.
This does not dishonor faithful pastors.
It actually honors the biblical purpose of pastoral ministry.
Because a faithful pastor does not want to become the destination of your faith.
He wants to point beyond himself.
Paul described Christ as giving leaders—including pastors and teachers—“for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ” in Ephesians 4:11–12.
Pastors matter.
Teachers matter.
Elders matter.
Discipleship matters.
Spiritual accountability matters.
Hebrews 13:17 takes spiritual leadership seriously enough to command believers to respond appropriately to those who watch over their souls.
So this is not an article about despising pastors.
It is about refusing to make pastors carry a weight that Jesus never asked them to carry.
Your pastor can preach the cross.
He cannot become the cross.
Your pastor can tell you about the blood of Christ.
He cannot shed blood that removes your guilt.
Your pastor can remind you that forgiveness is available.
He cannot purchase your forgiveness.
Your pastor can pray beside your hospital bed.
He cannot conquer death for you.
Your pastor can counsel you after your failure.
He cannot bear the wrath your sin deserved.
Your pastor can shepherd you toward the throne.
But only Jesus opened the way to it.
That distinction changes everything.
Because some people have quietly built their entire Christianity around access to another Christian.
They know how to ask the pastor to pray.
They know how to request counseling.
They know how to sit in a service.
They know when to say amen.
They know how to appear spiritually healthy.
But alone at 2:13 in the morning, when there is no worship team, no microphone, no pastor, no church crowd, and no one left to impress…
they do not know how to come trembling to Jesus.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe there is something you have been hiding.
Something you did.
Something you keep doing.
Something you promised God you would never do again.
And then you did it again.
You know the cycle.
Temptation.
Compromise.
Guilt.
Promises.
A few good days.
Then another fall.
Eventually you begin wondering whether God is tired of hearing your apologies.
So you search for somebody “more spiritual” to pray for you because somewhere inside you is the fear that Jesus may listen to them more willingly than He listens to you.
But hear what Hebrews says about Christ:
“Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.” — Hebrews 7:25, KJV
Read that again.
He ever liveth to make intercession for them.
The Greek uses the verb ἐντυγχάνειν — entynchanein, carrying the sense here of interceding or appealing on behalf of another.
Your hope does not ultimately rest in finding a human being holy enough to convince Jesus to care about you.
Jesus Himself intercedes.
The crucified and risen Christ is not reluctant to receive repentant sinners.
He is their Mediator.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Because Jesus does not mediate between God and humanity as a detached negotiator.
He gave Himself.
The very next verse after Paul identifies the “one mediator” says Christ Jesus “gave himself a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6).
The Mediator became the sacrifice.
The One standing between holy God and sinful humanity did not merely deliver a message.
He delivered Himself.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally about finding the right religious professional who can get you closer to God.
It is about God coming near to sinners in Jesus Christ.
Think about what happened when Christ died.
Matthew records that the veil of the temple was torn “in twain from the top to the bottom” (Matthew 27:51).
That direction matters.
From top to bottom.
God was not waiting for humanity to climb high enough.
Christ had opened the way.
Hebrews 10:19–22 therefore speaks of believers having boldness to enter through the blood of Jesus and urges them to “draw near.”
Draw near.
Not because you finally became impressive.
Not because your pastor knows your name.
Not because you belong to the perfect church.
Not because you accumulated enough good behavior to cancel the things you regret.
Draw near because of Jesus.
Maybe religion taught you to hide when you were dirty.
The Gospel tells repentant sinners where to run when they are dirty.
To Christ.
Maybe shame told you, “Stay away until you fix yourself.”
Jesus says the sick need a physician.
Maybe your failures have been whispering, “There is no way back after what you did.”
The cross answers, “It is finished.”
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
It says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and His grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly came to save sinners.
That is the scandal.
Holy God.
Guilty humanity.
And between them stands not our résumé, our church attendance, our pastor, our religious performance, or our reputation.
There stands a crucified Savior.
Jesus Christ.
This is why placing a pastor in the role of mediator is dangerous even when the pastor himself never asks for it.
Eventually, every human shepherd will disappoint you.
Some will misunderstand you.
Some will make mistakes.
Some will preach a sermon you disagree with.
Some will fail to notice your pain.
Some may leave a ministry.
Some may fall seriously into sin and require biblical accountability and discipline.
And when people have confused their pastor with their Mediator, a pastor's failure can feel like God's failure.
But Jesus is not your pastor's character flaw.
Jesus is not your pastor's bad decision.
Jesus is not your church hurt.
Jesus is not the hypocrisy somebody committed while carrying His name.
Human shepherds can fail.
The Good Shepherd remains faithful.
This matters deeply for people carrying church wounds.
You may have been hurt by somebody who preached Scripture.
You may have trusted someone who abused that trust.
You may have watched religious hypocrisy destroy something inside you.
And perhaps you walked away thinking:
“If that is Christianity, I want nothing to do with it.”
But before you walk away from Jesus because somebody representing Him represented Him badly, look at Jesus Himself.
Do not measure Christ by the worst behavior of someone who claimed His name.
Measure Christians by Christ.
The answer to pastoral idolatry is not pastoral hatred.
The answer to spiritual abuse is not pretending biblical spiritual authority does not exist.
The answer is putting every human authority underneath the authority of Jesus Christ and His Word.
A faithful pastor should be able to say, in the spirit of Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 11:1, follow me as I follow Christ.
Christ remains the standard.
Christ remains the center.
Christ remains the Head of His church.
Christ remains the Savior.
Christ remains the Mediator.
That also means you do not need celebrity access to have heavenly access.
Perhaps nobody important knows your name.
Maybe you will never sit at the table with a famous preacher.
Maybe your comment will never receive a response.
Maybe nobody will invite you onto a stage.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, obscurity on earth does not mean obscurity in heaven.
You can pray.
You can repent.
You can confess your sins to God.
You can open Scripture.
You can cry before Christ when nobody else knows you are crying.
You can whisper His name from a hospital room.
From a prison cell.
From a broken marriage.
From a bedroom where addiction has beaten you again.
From a car parked outside your house because you are afraid to walk inside and face what your choices have done.
You can come to Jesus.
Not casually.
Not arrogantly.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because the blood of Christ does.
And maybe that is what somebody reading this needs tonight.
Not another performance.
Not another religious mask.
Not another week pretending everything is fine.
Jesus.
If there is hidden sin, bring it into His light.
If repentance is necessary, repent.
If you have harmed someone, pursue biblical reconciliation where appropriate.
If you need wise pastoral counsel, seek it.
If you need mature believers around you, do not isolate yourself.
Christianity was never designed as solitary spirituality.
But understand the difference:
Christian community accompanies you to Christ.
It does not replace Christ.
Pastors shepherd you toward Christ.
They do not replace Christ.
Teachers explain the Word of Christ.
They do not replace Christ.
Brothers and sisters pray with you.
They do not replace Christ.
There is one Mediator.
And if this exposed the uncomfortable possibility that you have depended more on spiritual personalities than on the Savior Himself, do not hide behind embarrassment.
Bring even that to Jesus.
Somebody else may need evidence tonight that losing confidence in a person does not require losing confidence in Jesus.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not fifty random people.
One.
The friend who stopped attending church because a leader wounded them.
The believer who has become spiritually dependent on a personality.
The exhausted pastor who secretly feels pressured to become everything for everyone.
The person who thinks they are too filthy to approach God.
Send this privately if that would be wiser.
Because there may come a day when someone you admire disappoints you, and on that day you may need this reminder again:
Your pastor was never your foundation.
Jesus is.
Your pastor was never your Savior.
Jesus is.
Your pastor was never your Mediator.
Jesus is.
The purpose is not to build devotion to a personality. It is to keep pointing people toward biblical truth, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We will never put a price tag on access to Jesus.
Leave thinking about Jesus.
The One who knew your scandal before anyone else knew.
The One who saw the chapter you desperately wanted erased.
The One who did not excuse your sin but carried sin's judgment at Calvary.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still receives repentant sinners.
The One who intercedes.
The One who saves.
The One who remains when heroes fall, crowds disappear, churches disappoint, feelings fade, and your own strength finally runs out.
Your pastor may point you toward the door.
But Jesus is the reason the door is open.
And perhaps that is the sentence you should carry with you tonight:
When every human voice goes silent, the blood of Jesus is still speaking a better word over every sinner who comes to God through Him.
